evidence.quote: It keeps this heading as it passes through the red rock area of the Village of Oak Creek on its way to Sedona

evidence.claim: The Red Rock Scenic Byway winds through Sedona’s high-desert red-rock country.
evidence.quote: Red Rock Scenic Byway winds through Sedona's Red Rock Country

evidence.claim: high-desert red-rock country.
evidence.quote: Travelers are amazed by the high desert's power, diversity, and sense of intimacy with nature.

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration lists it as a 7.5-mile All-American Road and gives twenty minutes for the drive, with several hours for activities.
evidence.quote: Red Rock Scenic Byway All-American Road • Arizona Length 7.5 mi / 12.1 km Time to Allow Take 20 minutes to drive, but allow several hours to include all activities along the byway.

evidence.claim: Its description emphasizes the diversity of the high desert; Wikipedia records the 2006 designation as recognition of the red rock and sandstone formations along the road.
evidence.quote: In 2006, the United States Department of Transportation awarded SR 179 its highest designation within the National Scenic Byways Program: the All-American Road designation, due to the red rock and sandstone formations

evidence.claim: Its description emphasizes the diversity of the high desert
evidence.quote: Travelers are amazed by the high desert's power, diversity, and sense of intimacy with nature.

evidence.claim: Along the route, the Village of Oak Creek occupies an open area among red-rock buttes and canyons, surrounded by Coconino National Forest.
evidence.quote: Big Park, the pioneers' name for the large open area that became the Village of Oak Creek in the early 1960s, is set among scenic red-rock buttes and canyons.

evidence.claim: surrounded by Coconino National Forest.
evidence.quote: the town is surrounded by the Coconino National Forest.

evidence.claim: The number SR 179 first belonged to a different route, designated between 1935 and 1939 from SR 79 to SR 69 in Prescott Valley.
evidence.quote: The original SR 179 was designated between 1935 and 1939 from SR 79 (now SR 89A) to SR 69 in Prescott Valley.

evidence.claim: By 1960, that route had been canceled and the number assigned to the present road.
evidence.quote: By 1960, this route was cancelled, and SR 179 was designated on its current route.

evidence.claim: From I-17’s exit 298, SR 179 heads briefly northwest, then curves north toward the Village of Oak Creek.
evidence.quote: The southern terminus of SR 179 is at exit 298 off of I-17; the exit is about 15 miles (24 km) north of Camp Verde.  SR 179 heads northwest from the interchange briefly before curving towards the north.

evidence.claim: Bell Rock’s scenic area adjoins the village’s north end.
evidence.quote: The Bell Rock scenic area adjoins the north end of VOC

evidence.claim: Entering Sedona, the highway follows Oak Creek’s east bank and crosses the creek before ending at SR 89A.
evidence.quote: As it enters the Sedona city limits, it roughly follows along the east bank of Oak Creek.  It crosses the creek near Tlaquepaque Arts and Shopping Village, just before reaching its northern terminus at SR 89A.

evidence.claim: Bell Rock’s sedimentary layers lie in horizontal beds.
evidence.quote: Bell Rock is a butte composed of horizontally bedded sedimentary rock

evidence.claim: Bell Rock rises just north of the Village of Oak Creek, with Courthouse Butte immediately to its east.
evidence.quote: Bell Rock is a butte just north of the Village of Oak Creek, Arizona, United States, south of Sedona in Yavapai County. With an elevation at its summit of 4,919 feet (1,499 m), it is just west of Courthouse Butte.

evidence.claim: Horizontal beds of sedimentary rock make up the butte.
evidence.quote: Bell Rock is a butte composed of horizontally bedded sedimentary rock

evidence.claim: The hiking route described in Wikipedia reaches a small plateau on the northwest face.
evidence.quote: The most popular route is a moderate hike that reaches a small plateau on the northwest face of the butte.

evidence.claim: That plateau is below the summit: reaching the top requires a challenging, unmarked trail.
evidence.quote: A challenging unmarked trail must be taken to reach the summit.

evidence.claim: Cathedral Rock’s name has not always matched the map.
evidence.quote: Cathedral Rock was called "Court House Rock" on some early maps

evidence.claim: Some early maps labeled it Court House Rock, while the separate Courthouse Butte appeared as Church House Rock.
evidence.quote: Cathedral Rock was called "Court House Rock" on some early maps, and Courthouse Butte was called "Church House Rock"

evidence.claim: The sandstone butte stands about one mile west of SR 179 in Coconino National Forest.
evidence.quote: The rock formation is located in Coconino National Forest in Yavapai County, about 1 mile (1.6 km) west of State Route 179 (SR 179)

evidence.claim: A short, steep trail from Back O’ Beyond reaches the gaps between its rock formations.
evidence.quote: The Cathedral Rock trail (USFS Trail #170) is a popular short, steep ascent from the Back O' Beyond trailhead to the saddle points or "gaps" in Cathedral Rock.

evidence.claim: Ripple marks are visible along the lower trail, and a black basalt dike can be seen in the first saddle.
evidence.quote: Ripple marks are prominent along the lower Cathedral Rock trail, and a black basalt dike may be seen in the first saddle.

evidence.claim: The summit reaches 4,967 feet above sea level, while the described hiking route ends at the saddle points.
evidence.quote: The summit elevation of Cathedral Rock is 4,967 ft (1,514 m).

evidence.claim: while the described hiking route ends at the saddle points.
evidence.quote: from the Back O' Beyond trailhead to the saddle points or "gaps" in Cathedral Rock.

evidence.claim: A cross is both symbol and structure at the Chapel of the Holy Cross.
evidence.quote: The main feature of the chapel is a 90 ft (27.4 m) tall iron cross on the southwestern wall, which serves both aesthetic and structural purposes.

evidence.claim: Local rancher and sculptor Marguerite Brunswig Staude commissioned the chapel, built into Sedona’s red-rock buttes between 1954 and 1956.
evidence.quote: The Chapel of the Holy Cross is a Roman Catholic chapel built from 1954 to 1956 into the red rock buttes of Sedona, Arizona, within the Coconino National Forest. It was inspired and commissioned by local rancher and sculptor Marguerite Brunswig Staude

evidence.claim: August K. Strotz designed it, with Richard Hein as project architect.
evidence.quote: was designed by August K. Strotz of the firm of Anshen & Allen, with Richard Hein of the firm as the project architect.

evidence.claim: Workers moved upwards of 25 tons of rock without dynamite.
evidence.quote: Upwards of 25 tons of rock was moved without the use of dynamite.

evidence.claim: The walls were sandblasted inside and out to expose their textured aggregate, and gray glass reduces glare at the two ends.
evidence.quote: Inside and out, the walls were sandblasted to unveil the textured aggregate. To reduce glare, smokey-gray-colored glass is utilized at the two ends of the chapel.

evidence.claim: The approach continues the concrete work: a long, curved ramp of textured concrete leads from the parking area to the chapel.
evidence.quote: Upon arrival, visitors walk up a ramp from the parking area to the chapel. The long, curved ramp is constructed of textured concrete.

flags: ADOT corridor plan (00) and state designation list (02) contain archive headers only. They cannot verify the 1987 state designation date, original road construction or the catalog’s corridor-plan descriptions.
Wikipedia conflates the full SR 179 route with the 7.5-mile byway. FHWA confirms the byway length but not its endpoints; avoid saying the entire I-17–SR 89A drive is 7.5 miles.

Overview is shorter because the cache supplies little road history beyond reassignment of the highway number, and little road character beyond its northward curve and creek alignment. Bell Rock is kept short because its cache page is thin.
Archived FHWA mentions a $5 use pass at unspecified stops. No current pass or parking rules are cached; no practical fee claim included.
The chapel source calls the cross iron but also describes reinforced concrete walls and cross. Material of the cross omitted; its dual structural and aesthetic purpose is supported.

Current copy’s “whole drive is seven and a half miles” is omitted because the sources do not independently establish that mileage for the complete numbered-highway route. Sedona’s naming anecdote is supported but unrelated to the road’s history.
